items.prose: A strategy wins £1 on 55% of trades and loses £1 on the rest, independently. It makes 400 trades.
items.question: What is the standard deviation of the P&L after 400 trades? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\operatorname{Var}(S_n) = 4np(1 - p)$, then take the square root.

byKey.fair: £20 is the fair walk's $\sqrt{400}$. With $p = 0.55$ each step has variance $1 - 0.1^2 = 0.99$.
byKey.coin: You used $np(1 - p)$. A $\pm$£1 step is twice as wide as a 0-or-1 outcome, so multiply by 4.
byKey.var: 396 is the variance. Take its square root.

explain.text: Each trade has variance $4 \times 0.55 \times 0.45 = 0.99$, so 400 trades have variance 396. The standard deviation is about £19.90, against a mean of $400 \times 0.1 = $ £40.

items.prose: You start with £30 and make fair £1 bets until you reach £120 or go broke.
items.question: What is the chance you reach £120?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For fair bets, $P_i = \tfrac{i}{N}$.

byKey.ratio: You compared the distances, 30 to 90. The chance is your share of the whole range, $\tfrac{30}{120}$.
byKey.half: A fair game does not make both ends equally likely. The nearer end, £0, is more likely.
byKey.flip: 0.75 is the chance of going broke.

explain.text: First-step analysis gives $P_i = i/N$ for fair bets, so the chance is $\tfrac{30}{120} = 0.25$. On average the game lasts $30 \times 90 = 2700$ bets.

items.prose: Count paths of $\pm 1$ steps from $(0, 0)$ to $(12, 2)$.
items.question: How many of them touch level 4?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reflect to $(12, 2m - k)$ and count paths there.

byKey.all: 792 counts every path to $(12, 2)$. Only some reach 4.
byKey.to-four: 495 counts paths to $(12, 4)$. The mirror end is $2m - k = 6$, not the level itself.
byKey.diff: 572 is the number that never touch 4: $792 - 220$.

explain.text: With $m = 4$ and $k = 2$ the mirror end is $2m - k = 6$. A path to $(12, 6)$ has 9 ups and 3 downs, so there are $\binom{12}{9} = 220$. That is 220 of the $\binom{12}{7} = 792$ paths to $(12, 2)$.

items.prose: A share's daily log returns are independent with standard deviation 1.5%.
items.question: What is the standard deviation of its 16-day log return?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the daily standard deviation by $\sqrt{16}$.

byKey.linear: You multiplied by 16. Variances add, so the standard deviation grows by $\sqrt{16} = 4$.
byKey.daily: 1.5% is one day. Sixteen days spread further.

explain.text: Sixteen independent days have variance $16 \times (1.5\%)^2$, so the standard deviation is $1.5\% \times 4 = 6\%$.

items.prose: A player has an edge: each £1 bet wins with chance $p = 0.51$. She starts with £20 against a casino with endless money.
items.question: What is the chance she is eventually ruined? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Let $N \to \infty$ in $P_i = \dfrac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N}$ with $r = 49/51 < 1$.

byKey.certain: Ruin is certain only when $p \le \tfrac{1}{2}$. With an edge, $r < 1$ and $r^N \to 0$.
byKey.one-bet: 0.49 is the chance of losing one bet. Ruin needs her to lose 20 more than she wins.

explain.text: With $r = 49/51 < 1$, $r^N \to 0$, so $P_i \to 1 - r^i$ and the chance of ruin is $r^{20} \approx 0.4493$. Even with an edge, a £20 bankroll is ruined almost half the time.

items.prose: A fair walk takes 10 steps from 0.
items.question: What is $P(S_{10} = 0)$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ending at 0 needs exactly 5 ups among the 10 steps.

byKey.half: You expected a fair walk to be back at 0 half the time. It must have exactly 5 ups, which happens about a quarter of the time.
byKey.one-path: That is the chance of one particular path. Many orders of 5 ups and 5 downs end at 0.
byKey.eleven: You spread the chance evenly over 11 endpoints. They are not equally likely: the middle is the most likely.

explain.text: Ending at 0 needs 5 ups and 5 downs, in any of $\binom{10}{5} = 252$ orders. So $P(S_{10} = 0) = \tfrac{252}{1024} \approx 0.2461$, the most likely endpoint but far from certain.

items.prose: A price moves up or down one tick per minute, with equal chance. You know $P(S_{12} \ge 4) = 0.1938$ and $P(S_{12} \ge 6) = 0.0730$.
items.question: What is the chance it touches 4 ticks above its start within 12 minutes? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $P(S_n \ge m) + P(S_n > m)$, remembering that $S_{12}$ is even.

byKey.end-only: That counts only the paths that end 4 or more up. Paths that touched 4 and fell back count too.
byKey.double: You doubled $P(S_{12} \ge 4)$. Paths ending exactly at 4 have no mirror partner, so the second term is $P(S_{12} \ge 6)$.
byKey.beyond: That is only the second term. Add $P(S_{12} \ge 4)$.

items.prose: Now the odds favour you: each bet wins with chance $p = 0.55$. You have £5 and want £10.
items.question: What is the chance of reaching £10 with £1 bets? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: About 0.7317, far better than the 0.55 of one bold bet.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $r = \tfrac{0.45}{0.55}$ in $\dfrac{1 - r^5}{1 - r^{10}}$.

byKey.bold: 0.55 is one bet of £5. With the odds for you, many small bets let the edge work for you.
byKey.inverted: 0.2683 is the chance of going broke. Check that $r = q/p < 1$ here.

explain.text: $r = 0.45/0.55 = 9/11$ and $r^5 \approx 0.3666$, so $P_5 = \tfrac{1}{1 + r^5} \approx 0.7317$. With the edge on your side, small bets beat one bold £5 bet at 0.55. It is the mirror image of the casino case.

items.prose: A binomial model multiplies the price by $u = 1.2$ or $d = 1/1.2$ each day, from £100.
items.question: After 4 days with 3 ups and 1 down, in some order, what is the price?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $d = 1/u$, each down cancels one up.

byKey.added: You added 20% three times and took 20% off once. Multiply instead, with $d = 1/1.2$.
byKey.cube: £172.80 is three ups and no downs. The down move cancels one up.
byKey.ups-only: That is a net single up. Three ups minus one down is a net of two.

explain.text: With $ud = 1$ the price depends only on ups minus downs: here $3 - 1 = 2$, so $100 \times 1.2^2 = 144$. In logs this is a $\pm \ln 1.2$ walk sitting at $+2$.
